html:
The Punjab canal colonies were new farming districts that the British created in western Punjab between about 1885 and 1940, by digging great canals into dry grazing land between the rivers and settling farmers on it.

Before the canals, the land between the Indus tributaries was scrub used by herders. Canals fed by weirs on the rivers brought water all year round. The government then handed out plots to colonists, mostly experienced farmers from crowded central Punjab, and to retired soldiers. New towns were laid out on grids, among them Lyallpur, now Faisalabad.

The colonies became one of the richest farm regions in Asia, sending wheat and cotton by rail to the ports. In 1907 a law to tighten control over colonists set off protests, remembered in the song Pagri Sambhal Jatta. Bhagat Singh was born in a colony village that year.

The Partition of India in 1947 put most colonies in Pakistan, and Sikh and Hindu colonists fled east. Sharing the rivers then needed the Indus Waters Treaty. In the east, the Bhakra Dam carried on the work.
sum: The Punjab canal colonies were new farming districts that the British created in western Punjab between about 1885 and 1940, by digging great canals into dry grazing land between the rivers and settling farmers on it.
